div.p: Questions 19 to 26 are based on the following passage.

The first thing Adrian noticed when he stepped off the bus was the silence. The town of Sungai Merah had not changed much since he left ten years ago, yet it felt unfamiliar, as if time had rearranged it without his permission. The old clock tower still stood at the centre of the town but its paint was peeling, and the hands moved more slowly than he remembered. Adrian tightened his grip on his bag and wondered whether returning had been a mistake.

He had left Sungai Merah in search of something better. Fresh out of school, he believed that success could only be found elsewhere—in tall buildings, crowded streets and fast-paced lives. The town had seemed too small for his ambitions, too quiet for his dreams. When he boarded the bus that morning years ago, he promised himself that he would never look back. Yet here he was, returning for his late grandmother’s house, the last thing she had left behind.

The house stood at the end of a narrow lane, shaded by a mango tree that had grown taller over the years. As Adrian pushed open the creaking gate, memories flooded his mind when he saw the mango tree. He remembered sitting under it as a child, listening to his grandmother’s stories and believing that the world was full of possibilities. Those moments felt distant now, buried under years of deadlines, disappointments and silent struggles. Adrian worked in a big corporate company and had steadily climbed up the ranks. However, there were times when he wondered if it was all worth it.

Inside the house, dust covered the furniture and the air smelled of age and neglect. Adrian began sorting through old boxes, unsure of what he was searching for. Photographs, letters and faded notebooks lay scattered across the floor. The next few boxes contained old clothes that he decided to donate to charity. Then, in one corner, he found a small wooden box, beside a beautiful ceramic vase, he had never seen before. Curious, he opened it and discovered a leather notebook, its pages yellowed with time.

The notebook belonged to his grandmother. As Adrian flipped through the pages, he realised it was a journal. As he read the journal line by line, page by page, the minutes turned into hours. She had written about her hopes for her children and grandchildren, about her fears during difficult times and about her belief that everyone would eventually find their way, no matter how far they wandered. One sentence stood out to him: “Being lost is sometimes necessary, for it teaches us what truly matters.”

Adrian closed the notebook and sat in silence. For years, he had measured success by promotions and paychecks, yet he often felt empty. In chasing his dreams, he had lost touch with his family, his values and even himself. The journal made him realise that what he had been searching for was not a place but a sense of belonging.

Later that evening, Adrian walked through the town. He met familiar faces who greeted him warmly, despite the years of absence. The local café owner remembered his favourite drink and an old school friend invited him to catch up. With each conversation, Adrian felt a piece of himself returning, as if the town was quietly giving back what he had once lost.

Before leaving, Adrian visited his grandmother’s grave. He placed the notebook beside the flowers and whispered a thank-you. He understood now that life was not just about moving forward but also about knowing when to return. As the bus pulled away from the local bus station the next morning, Adrian looked out at Sungai Merah with a sense of peace. He had come back to settle a house, but he was leaving with something far more valuable—clarity, connection and the feeling of being found.
